meta.titre: Verb Patterns: choosing what follows the verb

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L English Language past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: Imagine a guard at a school gate in Yaounde. He tells a visitor, "The principal will let you enter after you sign." Replace *let* by *allow* and the sentence changes shape: "The principal will allow you to enter." These small shifts decide whether a sentence is correct in the Paper 1 grammar section, where one gap tests whether you know which form follows a given verb. Because the choice is made by the verb and not by the meaning, the safest method is to learn verbs in groups, as this lesson does.

items: An infinitive is the base form of a verb, with *to* (*to write*) or without it (*write*, the bare infinitive).
An -ing form is made from the verb by adding *-ing* (*writing*) and can act as a noun.
In *She told him a story*, *him* is the indirect object of the verb *told*.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Why the verb decides

In English the main verb decides which form must follow it: a to-infinitive (*to go*), a bare infinitive (*go*) or an -ing form (*going*). The pattern has to be learnt with the verb, because no general rule predicts it. A sentence such as *He decided going* is wrong not because of its meaning but because *decide* belongs to a different group.

| Pattern | Typical verbs | Example |
|---|---|---|
| verb + to-infinitive | want, decide, hope, plan, manage, refuse, promise, agree, fail, afford, learn, offer | She refused to answer. |
| verb + -ing | enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest, consider, risk, practise, admit, deny, postpone, delay | He avoided answering. |
| verb + object + to-infinitive | want, ask, tell, order, allow, advise, persuade, force, expect, invite, warn, remind | The coach advised them to rest. |
| verb + object + bare infinitive | make, let | The guard made us wait. |

### Make and let

After *make* and *let*, the object is followed by the bare infinitive, with no *to*: *They made him apologise. She let us leave.* In the passive, *make* takes *to*: *He was made to apologise.* *Let* has no common passive; we use *be allowed to* instead.

### Verbs of perception

After *see, hear, watch, feel* and *notice* we use an object and the bare infinitive when we saw the whole action, and an object and the -ing form when the action was in progress: *I saw him cross the road* (from start to finish), *I saw him crossing the road* (he was in the middle of it).

### Modals and fixed phrases

A modal verb is followed by the bare infinitive: *She can swim.* So are *had better* and *would rather*: *You had better leave. I would rather stay.*

### The suggestion trap

*Suggest* is followed by an -ing form or a *that* clause, never by an object and a to-infinitive: *He suggested taking the early bus* or *He suggested that I take the early bus*.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the verb is stop, remember, forget, try or regret
variantes.contenu_markdown: *Stop to + verb* means to interrupt one action in order to do another: *He stopped to buy water.* *Stop + -ing* means to end the action: *He stopped buying water.* *Remember to post it* is a task to do, whereas *remember posting it* is a memory of the past. The same contrast exists for *forget*. *Try to open* means to attempt, *try opening* means to test an idea. *Regret to inform* announces bad news, and *regret saying* expresses sorrow for an earlier act.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a phrase ends in to and is followed by a verb
variantes.contenu_markdown: In some phrases *to* is a preposition, so the verb after it takes -ing: *look forward to meeting, be used to waking up early, object to paying, be committed to learning*. Compare *used to* for a past habit, which is followed by the bare infinitive: *We used to walk to school.* Test: if you can put a noun or *it* after *to*, the verb takes -ing.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the sentence is turned into the passive
variantes.contenu_markdown: The object becomes the subject and the pattern after the verb stays: *They allowed us to leave* becomes *We were allowed to leave*, and *The guards made them wait* becomes *They were made to wait*.

sections.enonce_markdown:
Choose the correct option.

Our teacher allowed us ______ the library after school.

A) use   B) to use   C) using   D) for use

etapes.action: Identify the main verb and the words that follow it.
etapes.justification: The verb is *allowed*, followed by the object *us*, so the gap comes after a verb and an object.

etapes.action: Recall the pattern of the verb.
etapes.justification: *Allow* belongs to the group of verbs like *ask, tell, advise and order*: verb + object + to-infinitive. It is not like *let* or *make*, which take the bare infinitive.
The passive confirms the pattern: *We were allowed to use the library.* The *to* stays after the verb.
etapes.resultat_markdown: *to use* is in the passive too.

etapes.justification: A) is the bare infinitive, which follows *let*, not *allow*. C) -ing does not follow an object after *allow*. D) is not a verb form.
etapes.resultat_markdown: A, C and D are wrong.

etapes.justification: The completed sentence must sound natural and be grammatical.
etapes.resultat_markdown: *Our teacher allowed us to use the library after school.*

sections.conclusion_markdown: The answer is **B) to use**. *Allow* takes an object and a to-infinitive; the bare infinitive belongs to *let* (*Our teacher let us use the library*).

items.pourquoi_faux: *Avoid* belongs to the verbs followed by the -ing form, not the infinitive.

items.erreur_markdown: *The teacher let us to leave early.*
items.pourquoi_faux: After *let* the object is followed by the bare infinitive, without *to*.
In the active voice, *make* takes the bare infinitive. The *to* appears only in the passive.
items.correction_markdown: *They made him apologise.* or *He was made to apologise.*

items.pourquoi_faux: *Suggest* cannot take an object followed by a to-infinitive.
items.correction_markdown: *He suggested trying again.* or *He suggested that I try again.*

items.pourquoi_faux: In *look forward to*, the word *to* is a preposition, so the verb after it takes -ing.

items.enonce_markdown:
Choose the correct option.

She enjoys ______ stories to her little brother.

A) to read   B) reading   C) read   D) to reading
items.solution_markdown: *Enjoy* is followed by the -ing form. Answer: **B) reading**.

items.enonce_markdown:
Choose the correct option.

The manager let the staff ______ early on Friday.

A) to leave   B) leaving   C) leave   D) to leaving
items.solution_markdown: *Let* is followed by an object and the bare infinitive. Answer: **C) leave**. The other forms add *to* or *-ing*, which *let* does not take.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Explain the difference in meaning between *He stopped to buy water* and *He stopped buying water*.

(b) Rewrite in the passive: *The guards made the visitors leave their bags at the gate.*

(c) Correct the error in each sentence.
(i) I am looking forward to see you next week.
(ii) My father suggested me to take the early bus.
(iii) They refused answering the questions.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) *He stopped to buy water*: he interrupted what he was doing in order to buy water. *He stopped buying water*: he no longer buys water, so the action ended.

(b) **The visitors were made to leave their bags at the gate.** The bare infinitive of the active sentence becomes a to-infinitive in the passive.

(c) (i) **I am looking forward to seeing you next week.** (*to* is a preposition.)
(ii) **My father suggested taking the early bus.** (or *My father suggested that I should take the early bus.*)
(iii) **They refused to answer the questions.** (*refuse* takes the to-infinitive.)

items_markdown: The verb decides the form that follows it, so learn verbs in groups: to-infinitive, -ing form, object + to-infinitive, object + bare infinitive.
*Enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest* and *consider* take -ing; *want, decide, hope, manage, refuse* and *promise* take the to-infinitive.
After *make* and *let* use the object and the bare infinitive; the passive of *make* takes *to*.
*Stop, remember, forget, try* and *regret* change meaning with the to-infinitive and the -ing form.
Look at the word *to*: in *look forward to* and *be used to* it is a preposition and the verb takes -ing.
